utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume the hearing now, please have the accused brought in. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I see that the protective materials have been put into place, the Defence has been told about it. I now give you the floor, Mr. Harmon

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President and your Honours, this next witness is a protected witness only requesting protection of visual distortion. She will be using her name. In summary, Mr. President, she is a witness who is from the village of Gacice. If I could have the ELMO on, on the video monitor there should be for your Honours, the village should be appearing on the small map and the pointer is indicating on the monitor the location of this particular village where this witness is from. This village, Mr. President, is approximately two kilometres from the Hotel Vitez. This witness, who is name is Advija Hrustic, will testify what life was like in her village before the 1993 attack on her village. She will discuss intimidation and discrimination by the HVO in respect of Muslims in her community. She will also discuss the presence of soldiers from outside the Vitez municipality who wore distinct patches and who were located at the Dubravica school. When the time of April 16th 1993 arrives, she will be discussing her observations of attacks on adjacent villages, Ahmici, Donje Veceriska and others. She will describe the effect of the truck bomb in her village. She will discuss with your Honours events that are consistent with the pre-arming of Croats in her village and the evacuation of Croats from her village before the attack took place on 20th April 1993, and then she will describe the attack itself. Next she will testify, Mr. President and your Honours, about being taken prisoner by the HVO and how she and the other civilians were taken from her village to the Hotel Vitez, where they were placed around the Hotel Vitez in order to stop shelling of the Hotel Vitez. She will discuss her captivity for the remaining 16 days after she was returned from the Hotel Vitez to her village and she will discuss the conditions of her captivity and the plight of the other villagers. That is the summary, Mr. President and your Honours, of her testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Before the witness comes in, let us understand one another. The testimony must not be long. I cannot say this in front of the witness, because it would not be appropriate. The witness will express herself and then you only ask questions which would supplement what she has said according to the method which was applied with Witness A and with an abbreviation which would be much better. We can now have Ms. Advija Hrustic brought in. About how long have you planned for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well Mr. President, depending on how long she takes in her narrative, I would say no more than an hour and a half, but it is a question of how fast she goes through her narrative. I have instructed her to hit the important points in her narrative and I hope she will abide by my instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is fine, thank you. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please state your name and your first name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Advija Hrustic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The usher will give you the solemn declaration and you may remain seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead. MS. ADVIJA HRUSTIC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You have agreed to testify here, your face has been protected, the protective measures that you requested have been put into place in agreement with the parties. You will testify about what you saw, do it in your own words and after the Prosecutor asks you a few questions, you will then tell what are the important events about what happened. I mention again the important events that took place in Gacice, the intimidation campaign that preceded it, the things that took place after the truck bomb, the arming of the Croats, your captivity, what you observed among the military troops who surrounded you or who were merely with you. Once this has been done -- this can only been done once you have been asked questions. Do not worry if you lose the track of what you are saying, this is not an unusual thing in front of judges, the Prosecutor will put you back on the right road as to what you agreed. Mr. Harmon, some preliminary questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you. Ms. Hrustic, how old are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you born in Travnik and did you live from 1984 until 1993 in the Vitez municipality in the village of Gacice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In April 1993, did you live in that village with your husband and two small children, who were aged eight and four?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you and your husband of the Muslim religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In April 1993, was the village of Gacice, mixed Muslim Croat village, located approximately two kilometres away from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In 1993, were you employed as a teacher of the English language in the Vitez primary school, which was located in the city of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you also have a small general store in the village of Gacice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you please in your own words tell the judges what life was like in your village before the war, and also tell the judges when and why it changed, in your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war, when I lived in Vitez, the situation was very good, as it was in the entire country. We lived in a mixed village, we socialised, we went out together, we were godparents to each others' children. There was no difference between the two different religions, or whoever was which religion did not matter because people socialised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I see just a correction in the transcript, it says when you lived in Vitez, you mean when you lived in the village of Gacice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did that change and why did it change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right after the elections which were held in Vitez and the village where I come from, the Croats started to speak more clearly about -- there were Croats and Muslims did not belong to this town and to this state. Then one evening we were watching the Vance-Owen Plan being presented on television. Mr. Boban was also on TV, he said very clearly that the country was going to be divided, that the Croats belonged to one country, that they needed to follow these principles and that at this point they were a free people who can freely determine its own fate and that they needed to persevere in order to be who they really are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the Vitez municipality appear on a map, and if so which nationality would have control of the Vitez municipality, in that television programme you saw with Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vitez was clearly in the Croatian republic of Herceg-Bosna, and was supposed to be under the control of the Croatian defence council, that is the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After things started to change in the Vitez municipality, can you advise the court of what specific observations you saw that directly impacted on Muslims in their daily life? I can draw your attention to areas of work, of school, of events in the marketplace. If you could inform the court in your own words what happened in the Vitez municipality, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At first, the Croatian flags were put out on all the public buildings, private homes, so that the town was like at Christmas time. It was full of Croatian flags. In school, we had to speak the Croatian language. In the evening news, there was a caption saying, "the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna". There were many armed people around, and then we were all receiving our salaries in the Croatian money, the Kuna, and that was the only currency and this was how everything was paid in all the stores in the municipality. If by any chance in some store there were prices marked in Bosnian currency as well as Croatian currency, those stalls in the marketplace or those stores were blown up, the stalls were overturned, so there was no way to mark anything in the Bosnian currency and pay in any other than the Croatian one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In respect of the school where you taught, were you informed by the director of the school that instruction had to be in the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one morning the director came to me, they had had a meeting before I arrived, so I was not present at the meeting. That was the whole teaching staff and then he came over to me and he told me in person that this was a Croatian school of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and, "in this school, the only language spoken will be the Croatian language". In the staff room where we were all sitting, we had a picture of Mr. Franjo Tudjman, we had the Croatian symbols, that is Croatian flags also in this staff room.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the judges what happened to your husband in his work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband, up until then had worked -- I am not sure how long, but about eight years in the local commune, and that was part of the municipality, the municipal government. One day he came back from work and said that he was fired. Mr. Santic had offered him to sign off on a loyalty to the Herceg-Bosna, and then the gentleman pulled out a paper, a notice and said that he was no longer employed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me clarify something you mentioned about the marketplace. You said that if items were sold in Kuna and Bosnian money, there would be consequences to the stall owners. Did you personally see those incidents and can you describe them in detail to the judges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was personally on the marketplace one day, it was just a regular market day, there were a lot of people there. Suddenly, from the street we were surrounded by the policemen and the soldiers of the HVO, I do not know exactly how many there were. We were all afraid at that moment. Two of them were at the corners of the market, and so nobody could either enter the market or leave. They then passed by the stalls where the goods were being sold and wherever they saw that the prices were marked in both money they would overturn it, so all the stalls that displayed two currencies, they were overturned. So a friend of mine who also had a store at the marketplace, he had it also marked in Bosnian currency and his premises were blown up. All the windows were smashed, and he tried displaying both currencies and that did not help, then the same thing happened and then he tried marking it in German Marks and then had the same consequences. After that, he closed down his business.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You said that policemen came into the shops, into the marketplace and turned over these stalls. What kind of policemen were those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What insignia did those policemen have on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wore HV and HVO and they had white belts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now I would like to turn your attention to another area of your testimony. It is the area, if you could inform the judges what unusual events you observed in and around your village and in and around Vitez before the attack itself that occurred in your village on April 20th. What strange things occurred? Specifically if I could direct your attention to any training that you saw near your village, any unusual activities late at night that took place in your village. Could you tell the judges, please, what you saw in respect of those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, before the attack to our village, we could often observe a lot of armed individuals. They would be in groups of about 50 individuals, and they had, I do not know, the word -- I cannot recall, the word "target" in the Bosnian language. They all were armed and they were going to a nearby pool where they had target practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say "individuals", are you referring to HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the HVO soldiers who had clear insignia, they had the chequer-boards on their heads also, on their arms, on their jackets. Also at night I could observe from my window, at home, my first door neighbour, who was a Croat, who was almost always wearing a black uniform, he had the HVO insignia on his uniform. They were coming in different vehicles and they were hauling in things. It looked like big bags with handles like duffel bags. When they would come close to the house where they were leaving these things, they would turn off all the lights in the house, in the vehicle, but we could see this because sometimes there was moonlight and this would all usually happen between midnight and 2.00 am. Later, I could see this neighbour, after the war had started, that this neighbour was bringing out weapons from this house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: One last question of clarification on this point: how often would you see this unusual activity take place in your village before the attack on your village took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no specific time limits, we never knew when exactly this would happen, sometimes that would be two or three times a month, sometimes two or three times a week, sometimes night after night this would go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now if I could direct your attention to the presence in the Vitez municipality of some soldiers from the Dubravica school. Would you please inform the judges, first of all who these soldiers were, as far as you knew, what they did in the Vitez municipality in your community and what you did in respect of those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For instance in operations like the thing at the marketplace, and during the patrols in the town, Vitez is a very small town and everybody knows everybody else. We could see these soldiers patrolling together with the HVO soldiers. They were in the Princip factory, people of all, I think, groups were working there and our own people were able to tell us that there were a number of unknown people in uniforms who supposedly came there to provide security for the factory. Also, the school which was later moved to Vitez, there too we could often see soldiers and we could hear them talk. They had a different accent from us, and we could often see them going up and down the road, or in front of the school, and they were doing exercise, physical exercises and they were all armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What kind of insignia did they have on their uniforms, these soldiers from outside of the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had the HV and a kind of a leaf on their arm, like a branch, like branches.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You said that you saw these soldiers participating in operations with other HVO soldiers. Did you also see them at checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the entrance to our village, which was very close to the town, very often they would set up checkpoints and we would all be controlled, our documents would be controlled, our vehicles, bags would be searched to all of us, and these soldiers also participated in this, together with the soldiers from the Vitez area whom we did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the soldiers with the oak leaf, did they also participate with the HVO military police in operations that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just some other points of clarification on these soldiers who were stationed at the Dubravica school. Did they generally contribute to the intimidation of Muslims? Could you see them doing certain actions, could you hear them, what they were saying and if so, could you please describe fully to the court what you saw and what you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People were more than afraid in this kind of situation when we would see them and in these situations, that if we, say, went to school, we only saw the military, if we went to the marketplace, there were only the military around. If we went to the factories there were only military around in large groups. It was not just fear, it was terror.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Hrustic, I would like you to try to give a narrative answer to the judges. When I ask you about a particular subject area, in your own words and at your own pace, would you please inform the judges, without my interrupting, if you can, and I will be glad to assist you with certain questions, but I think the court is more interested in hearing you expound on some of these subjects than my asking you questions. Please, if you could fill in as many details as you could about these particular soldiers and what you did in terms of these soldiers, in terms of telephoning the Dubravica school and why you did that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People were simply scared, we all lived in terrible fear. We were afraid to say that we were Muslims, we were afraid to go out anywhere, because some of the people who lived around us may recognise us and kill us. They would recognise us for who we were. I had two children at that time, and knowing that the HVO military -- sorry, that the military were accommodated in the school in Dubravica, I did not know what to do. Out of fear, out of terrible fear for my children, one day I called up and I introduced myself as Maria, and I said, "are you really here to help us kill all the Muslims?", and the gentleman who answered the call said something to the effect, "do not be afraid any more, we are here now and your problems will be solved very soon. There is a reason why we came here", and so to the effect that the situation would be resolved soon. Very often, almost all Muslim families were receiving phone calls, that it was time for us to leave, that this was not our country, that we should go to Iraq, that we should go to Turkey, that this was the Croatian Republic, that we were not a nation, that we would all be killed, not just myself but all people, so in fear we would go to one another to ask what would happen. On one occasion, I personally was visiting a friend who called me almost daily, completely panicked, she was almost beside herself with fear, from all these phone calls. I went over to her and when the phone rang, she was just too afraid to pick it up. I picked it up, there was a male voice on the other end and, "the time has come for them to leave, they would be killed, they had no chance, time has run out for them", things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me clarify some of what you just told the judges. You said you called some people up. Did you call the school at Dubravica where the soldiers with the green leaves on their soldiers were located and did you speak to one of those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What exactly did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me that they had come from Herzegovina, that they had come from Grude, they had come to help, to help the Croats, that very soon everything was going to be the way it should be, and that I should not be afraid of anything, that the problems would be -- problems with the Muslims would be solved very soon. I had asked him whether they had come to kill all the Muslims and then he said, "yes, we will solve that very soon".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now I would like to turn to another area I would like you to tell the judges about and that is the time-frame from 16th April to 19th April and that is when you observed -- starting when you observed the village of Ahmici attacked and neighbouring villages. Could you please tell the judges where you were and what you saw? Please take your time in telling the judges what you saw.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The day before the attack on Ahmici was almost normal. I went to school and the children had a full day at school. We came back and then in the morning, some time around 5.50, we heard a couple of shells falling. We were afraid, we got up and since my house is on high ground, I could see almost the entire town below me. I saw the village of Ahmici in flames, I saw terrible smoke coming from the direction of that village. You could hear the shells exploding, you could smell the smoke. I heard the shells in the Stari Vitez, and we could even see the place where the shells would fall, the people were afraid. We called each other, asking if anybody knew what was going on, was this a war, was it something else? We had no idea what was happening. After that, I saw the surrounding villages in flames. I heard the shells. A village across, away from us in the other clearing was also shelled. We had no soldiers in the village, we had six or seven soldiers who went to the front-lines with the Serbian Army, and they would usually come back to the village without their weapons. They were all in civilian clothes in the village. We watched the village of Veceriska, how people are struggling around their houses. We saw one by one going up in flames. People were calling us over and asking for help. We had no way to go out and help them, but we organised for the women and children to move towards the houses that were closer to the forest, because that would be easier for escape. The night before the 20th, so on the 20th in the evening, the small arms fire in Veceriska village subsided, there was military there, but we could not see any children or women, we could only see the flames. In the morning, we pulled back to the upper area near the forest, there were three or four houses there where the women and children were sheltered. These were shelters which had 30 or maybe 10 people, women, children and the elderly. There were a few men left in the village, and they had dug up some trenches that were about 1.4 metres deep for cover. They did not have any weapons, my husband had blue jeans and a blue jacket and he had a hunting rifle, he had been a hunter for 20 years. He had two young men with him, 16 and 17 of age. They had two hand grenades and so in front of every house we had a couple of people who would guard these shelters where the women and children were, and from all sides, we were surrounded by the Croatian settlements, a factory was on one side, so it was impossible for us to leave. In the morning, at around 5.30 to 5.50, we heard our own village being shelled. The shells were falling from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Hrustic, before we get into the attack on the village on 20th April, let me clarify some things you have testified about. You said you could see surrounding villages in flames. Which villages were those? Can you identify them by name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the village of Ahmici, I saw Veceriska, I saw the houses in the old Vitez, I saw the surrounding villages whose names I really do not know on the other side. Those were the settlements close to the Veceriska village, because they had the upper and lower Veceriska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You also said that you saw some villages shelled. Did you see Stari Bila shelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that Stari Bila was being shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Being shelled from an artillery piece located where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could see very clearly from the balcony of my house, this was a house which was in the Croatian settlement across the way, and this was in the ground floor of a house that was still under construction. You could see the flame from where it was fired, so it was shelled from Mlakici to Stari Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At some point in time after the attack on Vitez and Stari Vitez took place, was there an enormous explosion that you felt in your village, and can you describe, please, to the judges, what effect that explosion had on your village, which was about two kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We heard the shelling, the fire and then there was a very powerful explosion. One had the feeling that the house was coming down. On my house, the glass, together with the frame, came down and a balcony door also fell to the floor from the explosion. The house was shaking as if it was going to tumble down. All the glass panes in the surrounding houses were broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you one other question about your previous testimony. Earlier you said you had made a telephone call to the Dubravica school to talk to soldiers who were wearing these green-leafed insignia. Do you remember approximately when that telephone call was made, what month?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I wonder whether you already asked that question, Mr. Harmon. I think you have. I think she said that she does not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is fine, Mr. President. Let me proceed to the events still before the attack on your village on April 20th. Were you aware of an ultimatum by the HVO to the men in your village to turn in their weapons and can you please in your own words tell the judges about that ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, our men were in the upper part of the village, and the HVO wanted a meeting with them. They told them that they had an ultimatum to surrender our weapons, that we had to sign an oath of allegiance to the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, that all the people needed to be disarmed. Our men refused this, asking the HVO army that they too should surrender their weapons, together with us, and that we should form mixed groups of Bosnians and Croats to organise guard duty over the weapons if they did not trust one another, but the HVO refused. They just insisted that our side should surrender whatever it had. Two days later, the Bosnian side initiated a meeting, asking that some kind of a compromise be reached, but they refused. They said that they had given us a chance, we had refused it and there was nothing more to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just a couple more points of clarification. Approximately how many men were in your village at or about April 20th 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where were the other men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our other men were on the first front-line against the Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What kind of weapons were available, did your men have in the village prior to the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the attack on the village, we had hunting rifles, we had a couple of grenades. It was mostly just hunting weapons, and some adjusted weapons that had been brought in maybe -- there were not more than five. I do not remember exactly how many, but I do not think there were move five.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On 19th April, the day before the attack, did you see Croat residents of Gacice leaving the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 19th April I was able to see Croatian women with their children and bags in great haste going towards the lower part of the village, that is in the direction of Mlakici village. Before that, I saw them during the previous weeks and months bringing in large quantities of food to store in their houses. All the women and children abandoned the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification, when you say Mlakici village, that is the Croatian part of the village of Gacice, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now Mr. President, if I can turn to Prosecutor's next exhibit, which is I believe 156, I ask that that be presented to the witness so she can refer to it if she wants in her description of the attack on April 20th. For the record, Mr. President, this is an exhibit which is a portion of Exhibit 77, it is an enlargement with certain numbers and circles indicating locations on it. It has attached to it a legend. For the record, Mr. President, the witness has had an opportunity to indicate to me these locations which have been marked on the exhibit. She has also had an opportunity to compare the legend with the numbers that are marked on the exhibit itself, and if I can ask her one question briefly? Ms. Hrustic, are the numbers on this particular exhibit that have been marked, and the descriptive material that is on the legend, have you had a chance to review both the numbers and the legend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is the legend accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please, if you feel comfortable using this particular exhibit during the course of the next part of your testimony, feel free to do so, otherwise I will ask you some questions about it later on. What I would like to do now, Ms. Hrustic, is to move on to the attack itself on your village that took place on 20th April. Can you please describe to the judges in your own words, at your own pace, the attack, what happened, what you saw and what you did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The night before the actual attack, from the house marked with the number 1, I went to another house marked number 6, with my two children, my mother, because there were other people there. The shelling started in the morning, of the village itself, from three sides. One direction came from number 12, and from Mlakici, which is also marked with number 12. There was a lot of fire in the morning, the shells were falling and our men, who had no weapons, were withdrawing towards the woods, whereas the women and children stayed in the cellars. After the shelling, I went out a couple of times to bring water for the children because we had not prepared anything in the basements. I could see the army, the military, people in uniform running between the houses, calling out to each other, calling us out, shooting. We stayed in the shelters and I heard from the direction marked here as 11, women and children crying, screaming. Then there were bursts of fire again, the military, the soldiers that I could hear speaking would shout "balijas", they would curse our mothers, they would threaten us, "come out, we know you are there, we will slaughter your women and children, nobody will remain alive. Do not hide, there is no point, we know you are there", and with a group of eight that I was one of, there was an elderly man of about 65. The rest were my two children and some elderly women. We came out of the basement, which is marked as number 6. While we were still in the basement I heard bursts of fire, and I could see some houses because there was no doors where I was, I could hear a burst of fire, the glass breaking and then a house burning. There was an awful lot of smoke, almost all the surrounding houses were burning and the man calling us was behind the garage where we were staying and we could hear him clearly, we could hear him cocking his rifle, firing into glass and the flame that would appear a moment later. So I came out with the group, because we thought we would be safer if there were more of us in a group, and on the road, there were many children, many women, many old people; there were very many soldiers who had insignia, some of them had the letter U, some had HVO insignia, some had HV and there were a couple with the word Jastrebovi, "the hawks". They started laughing at us, "we knew you were there, you balija", they would push us around and they said, "go down the road now". They were around us, so we headed in a large column, a large line. There was an old imam with us who was about 60, over 60. A soldier took his rifle and said, "what do you balija want? You have come here to teach them how to be better balijas". The man said nothing except, "do not, my son". He took a pistol, put the pistol in his mouth, the man fell to his knees, he hit him a couple of times. He held this pistol in his mouth, threatening to kill him, saying that he should follow the column. We all of us reached a house where we were told that we would be going on. We did not know where we were going. They took us in front of the Vitez hotel, all the women and children --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you right there for just a minute to get some additional clarification. The soldiers that you saw in the village attacking your village, you said had a variety of different insignia, HVO, HV, the letter U. Did they also have Vitezovi patches on them, some of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the soldiers from those different units appear to be working together in the attack on your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the attack on your village come from three different directions which are indicated by the number 12 on Prosecutor's Exhibit 156?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At some point in time on 20th April, you said you and certain number of civilians from your house left and you joined other civilians and you were walked into the town of Vitez in a large column. Approximately how many civilians were in that column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were 247 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you told why you were being marched down to the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While you were en route to the Hotel Vitez, could you hear shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all the way we could hear shelling. The children were terrified, they would hide behind us, we heard rifle fire and shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me show you -- I am sorry. You then arrived at the Hotel Vitez, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of the Hotel Vitez, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me now ask the usher to please put on the ELMO Prosecutor's Exhibit 157, which will be two photographs, Mr. Usher. If I could start with the first photograph. The first photograph, Mr. Usher, is marked PH 206. Ms. Hrustic, do you recognise this photograph and can you tell the judges where this is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This is the Vitez hotel, where the civilians were taken on that day. That is exactly the spot where we were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if I could then have photograph 207 placed on the ELMO. Ms. Hrustic, do you recognise this photograph? What is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is the place where I was sitting that day with the other people, that was where they took us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So you were sitting between the Hotel Vitez, which is in photograph 206, and this particular building, which is photograph 207, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now if I could have, Mr. Usher, if you could next take Prosecutor's Exhibit 158 and place that on the ELMO, and for the record, Mr. President and counsel, this is an enlargement of a portion of Exhibit 45, and it has a legend with one item indicated on the legend. Ms. Hrustic, do you see on your monitor Exhibit 158 that has been placed on the ELMO? Can you tell the judges what the large white circle is with the number 1 next to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the area where we spent two and a half to three hours on 20th April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So that is the area where about 247 civilians were kept on 20th April, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In your own words, Ms. Hrustic, would you tell the judges about your arrival at the Hotel Vitez and what occurred while you were at the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got there, we were standing and waiting, we did not know what to do. There were some men with us and they first told us that all the men should go to one side and that the women and children to another side, so there would be a metre or two between the two of us, the two groups, and then they took away the men. This was all happening within maybe ten minutes. Then we went on standing and then we sat down and a soldier said, "I am going inside to inform the commander about this", and he pointed with his head in our direction. One of the soldiers said, "we could put them in the cinema". There was a shell crater in front of the hotel, and I sat inside. The soldiers were coming in and out of the hotel. There were no particular shifts or anything like that. Then a soldier came, there was a man who came first with a camera, and then a soldier came out who had a crate of mineral water, and said, "you see how good we are". The women and children started to drink water, the cameraman filmed all this and as soon as he left, the crate was taken away from the women and the children.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You said the soldier said, "I am going inside to inform the commander". Were there any other comments by the HVO soldiers talking about shelling and the location of the civilians in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One of the soldiers said, while we were standing there, "you are going to sit here now and let your people shell you, because they have been shelling us up to now, and you better sit down and wait".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the soldiers stay with the 247 civilians or after the soldiers said that, did the soldiers retreat into the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hotel is mostly of glass, so that we could see them and they could see us. They said that they had good shelters in the hotel, that they were not afraid, no one could harm them, so the soldiers brought us there and went inside and they were there while the filming took place, whereas the rest of the time, a couple of them watched us through the glass and we were told that if anybody moved, they would be shot on the spot because they could see us and they were watching us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You remained there for about two and a half to three hours, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we sat there. They did not tell us to go any place, and we did not know where to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you later told where you should go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, later we were told to go back to the village, and as we were passing through the village, we saw that almost all the houses were on fire, the stables were on fire, we were afraid, we did not have anywhere to sleep because this was a large group of people. One of the soldiers turned around and said, "what do you want? You want me to kill you all here and now?"

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you escorted back to your village on your own free will, or were you threatened that if you did not go back to your village you would be killed, at the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you explain that answer, please, to the judges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly all the women and children who had left the village had no food on them, no water, nothing. Each one of the women were just holding on to their children by the hand and when we got there, we did not know what to eat, where to go back to, and we did not have anywhere to go back to in the village, because the village was burning. We saw it, we had passed through it, so then we were told that we had to go back to Vitez, otherwise we would all be killed in front of the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you believe that you and the other civilians who were gathered around the Hotel Vitez were there as human shields?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You went back to your village and remained in your village for approximately 16 days, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You and the other civilians were placed in a number of houses that had not been destroyed and those are indicated on Prosecutor's Exhibit 156 with the number 4 and the radiating arrows that point to a variety of houses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While you were in that village of Gacice during those 16 days, I would like you to tell the judges first off about a trench that you saw being dug. Will you please explain to the judges what you saw in respect of that trench?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, I am not getting an English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got back to the village we were told to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is fine, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got back to the village, we were told that we had to stay in these houses that were in a group, so that they could see us, and that we could be under control. There was a checkpoint at the junction below those houses where armed military men were on guard. For that time, we never got any food or water or clothing. One morning, we did not have any water, so we had to cover a distance of some 200 metres, but after having informed the HVO soldiers who were there, or rather after asking them for permission to go and get water, and then we would go in groups of three or four women with cans to fetch water. From the house I was in, I was able to see my house, which is number 1, and we had to pass along that path to fetch water. A big trench digger arrived one day, which dug up in the Muslim grebje an enormous trench, maybe 40 or 45 metres long, and it was about two metres wide. We did not know why. One morning, I got up very early, I was going to fetch water, and I could see a white car, an ambulance, and a woman in a white coat, a man next to her, who lowered two bodies there. One was a little longer than half a metre, the other was a little bigger. Both were charred. I went back and asked my neighbour, "are we going to fill up those holes?"; in other words, were those holes for the rest of us inhabitants? He said that the body was of a little girl and her mother from Ahmici, he did not mention the name, he said that he was just following orders and if he is told that we should fill up that hole, he was sorry but that would happen; if not, then we would survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was your neighbour an HVO soldier by the name of Boro Krizanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did you make those observations of the two victims from Ahmici being put in the burial trench in your village; what date, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was towards the end of April, beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did Boro Krizanovic inform you of what units had participated in the attack on Gacice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said when we went back in front of the hotel that they were very good men, they had very good army, that they had received assistance, that the 303rd Split Brigade and the 125th Varazdin Brigade had come to their assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were those units from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did Boro Krizanovic also tell you about what had happened to a Muslim by the name of Fikret Hrustic who lived in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. What would happen to us, we asked them and how could they have done something like that, because this was so cruel. We found a man burnt in the basement of a house opposite the way to mine, he said that he was in front of the house, that Fikret Hrustic was inside, that he had lined up his pots and pans in front of the door, thinking that they would not come in, that he was yelling, saying "this will not be Herceg-Bosna" and that he did not want to come out. They said they could call him to come out, that he did not want to come out, that he shouted that this would never be Herceg-Bosna, "if I have to die, I will die here, this is my country", and then they set fire to him. He screamed while he was dying and then he fell silent. He said that Fikret was mad, he could have done without that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have my next exhibit, which is Exhibit 159, which I would like to distribute. It is a photograph of a headstone of Fikret Hrustic with relevant birth date and death date indicated on it. I have shown this to the witness, Mr. President, and I can move on then without putting it on the ELMO. Next I would like to turn to a gentleman by the name of Garic Kreso. Can you please, Ms. Hrustic, tell us about Mr. Garic Kreso; who he is, what conversations you had with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Upon our return in front of the hotel, a man who had a bullet-proof vest and a helmet on his head said his name was Kreso Garic, his parents were in the village of Mlakici. He said he had been living for 18 years in Zagreb, that he had come for the purpose of this operation to our village, and to the area, and that when the operation was completed, he would be going back to where he had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you aware of his going down to the Hotel Vitez at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told us that we should ask whatever we needed, that we should ask him for everything, no one was allowed to move from one house to another without asking him for permission, and in a number of cases, when we wanted anything, wanted to ask him something, then they would say that Kreso was not there for the moment, that he was in the hotel, that they had an important meeting and that when he came we could ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, Ms. Hrustic, I would like to turn your attention to Prosecutor's Exhibit 156, which is this enlargement of a portion of Exhibit 77. There appear to be in that photograph a number of homes, houses and structures that are burned, damaged. Have you had an opportunity to inspect this particular photograph before coming into court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There are a number of structures that are not indicated by numbers, but that are damaged. Can you tell the court whether those structures that are unnumbered but damaged are structures belonging to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is there one structure that belongs to a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In respect of this particular exhibit, you have had an opportunity to review photographs that were taken in the village of Gacice. If I could show you very quickly, with the assistance of the usher, a series of photographs, could you tell me who owned these particular structures, please? I can start with Exhibit 78 and we will move very quickly through these. They will be placed on the ELMO and they will appear in front of you, starting with photograph 254, Mr. Usher? Let me just expedite this. If there is no objection from counsel, 254, is this the home belonging to Nurberg Hrustic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now if we could move to 256, does this structure belong to Ferid Subasic, a Muslim in the village of Gacice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could move to photograph 250, please? Is this building located in Gacice and did it belong to two sisters by the name of Subasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now Mr. Usher, I have concluded with that exhibit. If we could go to Exhibit 160, please, which is the Prosecutor's next exhibit? Starting, Mr. Usher, photograph 238 from Exhibit 160. Ms. Hrustic, is this the photograph of the small mosque that was in the village of Gacice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now if we could turn to photograph 241, Mr. Usher. Is 241 a house also located in Gacice that belonged to Ekrem Herzegovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now if we could turn to photograph 252, please, is this a structure in Gacice belonging to a man by the name of Ismir Hrustic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Imsir Hrustic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if I could go to photograph 254? You showed me, did you not, three homes that were in Gacice, but you did not know the names of the owners but you said these were Muslim homes. Is this one of those photographs which is photograph 254?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we turn to photograph 256, please, Mr. Usher? I will ask you the same questions, is this a house that belonged to a Muslim and is located in the village of Gacice. Let us get the photograph on the ELMO first. It does not appear to be in there. Okay, can we turn to 250 then? Mr. President, I am not sure why those photographs do not appear in that exhibit, but I will present them at a later time. Now if we could turn to Exhibit 261.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am not sure that any of this is being contested by the Defence. Mr. Hayman, are you contesting any of these? You are putting this into the record, recognised by the witness. It is like the map. Do it the way you did with the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell me what this exhibit is, please, Ms. Hrustic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the entrance to a building in the village of Gacice which was a cultural centre before the war, a kind of youth centre with a discotheque and a library.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Prior to the April 20th attack, there appears to be some graffiti on this photograph. Was that graffiti on that building prior to the 20th April 1993 attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was there for at least three months on the building prior to the attack. We were not allowed to enter the building, the key was taken away from us. The Croatian army was there, and in front of this door, there were two armed guards. In the evening also they would bring in something, I do not know what. In any event, Muslims were not allowed to enter this building and these are the graffiti on that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no additional questions. Thank you, Ms. Hrustic. I would like to move to introduce into evidence, Mr. President, Exhibit 156 and the legend; 157, which is two photographs; 158, which is an aerial enlargement of the area around the Hotel Vitez; 159 and 160, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise. I have one additional question of the witness which my colleague indicated. Thank you. Can you tell me how you left the village of Gacice 16 days later and how the other villagers left the village? I am talking about the Muslim villagers who had been detained in these various houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, while we were in the village, armed men would come into the village on trucks and they had lists of names of people and they would read out the names on the list, they would take the women and children whose names they would read and take them away, we do not know where. On that day, a friend from the HVO army came and said to me that I should take my two children and my mother and that he would take me to the territory under the control of the Bosnian army. The other people who stayed behind in the village, the other women, they did not know where I was going and I was not told exactly. About two hours later, they were put on a truck and they were told that they should go to Vjetrenica and from there on foot together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So the other villagers were taken to the Dubravica checkpoint and told to go on foot to Zenica, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were all told to go to Zenica, and only then did we learn that the others had been also taken to various sites, various places according to this list, but we did not know at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, that does not change your point as far as the cross-examination is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I turn to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, maybe we must have misunderstood one another. I do intend to cross-examine this witness, but I have no objections to the admission of these exhibits. I have quite a number of questions, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Nobilo, it is 5.40, we will now adjourn and resume tomorrow at 11.00. (5.40 pm)

procedural_notes.text: Page 4688 to 4785 redacted - in closed session
(Hearing adjourned until 11.00 am the following day)
